label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
output:
Kelechi Obi, my guy.

You said if I was serious I should put it in writing, so here it is. A proper letter. Not a voice note. Stamp, envelope, the whole circus. I posted it to Croydon on purpose. If you’re reading this on the train and someone sees you smiling, tell them it’s a bill.

At my birthday you were doing your usual: quantity surveyor, nine years at the same firm in Croydon, same spreadsheet, same look on your face like you’re waiting for the clock to release you. I said come and teach maths. You laughed like I’d asked you to run a marathon in slippers. Then you said if I was serious, put it in writing. So I’m serious.

I’m not going to preach at you. You hate that, and I’m not very good at it. This is just what I see.

You got an A in further maths, and you were the one tutoring half our hostel in Moremi before exams. Not because anyone made you. Because you could explain things in a way that didn’t make people feel small. I remember that. You’d break something down, someone would say “ohhhh” and you’d move on. That’s not nothing. That’s most of the job, honestly.

You did the same thing with my nephew at Christmas. Fractions, plates, jollof rice portions. He still talks about it. Not because he loves fractions, but because you made it make sense. He felt clever that day. That’s what teaching is. You don’t need a cape. You just need to be patient enough to show someone the thing they’ve decided they can’t do.

Our school has 1,100 kids and two Year 9 maths groups have had a supply teacher since September. I’m not saying you’re the saviour of Peckham. I’m saying there’s a real need, in a real school, and you’re the sort of person who could actually do it. One person doesn’t fix a timetable. But one decent person in front of a class makes a difference to that class. That’s not a slogan. It’s just true.

The route I’m talking about is the salaried one. You’d be in school, training, getting paid, one year, starting September 2027. Applications for that intake open soon. There’s an open evening on Thursday 19 November 2026, 6pm, at the training partnership in Lewisham. I can go with you. That’s the whole ask. Not “quit your job tomorrow”. Not “sign your life away”. Just come and listen. You can sit at the back with your arms folded like you’re doing me a favour.

Now the money. Yes, first year pay is a drop. I’m not going to pretend it isn’t. But holidays, pension, and it goes up. You’re 34, not 94. You can take a hit for one year if it leads somewhere you actually want to be. And before you say age: a woman in my department started at 41. You’ve got time. You just feel old because you’ve been in the same chair for nine years.

I’m also not going to lie to you about the job. Teaching is hard. Marking is endless. Some days behaviour is pure wahala. When I started in 2019 I cried in the car park twice in my first term. I’m not hiding that. It gets better, but not because it suddenly becomes easy. It gets better because you get better, and because the good days start stacking up.

Last month a Year 11 boy called Damola finally got simultaneous equations after three weeks. He shouted “is that all??” and the whole class clapped. You can’t put that in a cost report. That sound stays with you. It’s worth more than a spreadsheet, even on the days when the spreadsheet is looking very attractive.

You said on your last birthday that you just want to do something that matters before 40. I’m not saying teaching is the only thing that matters. It isn’t. But it’s one of the few jobs where you can see it happen in front of you. You explain something, a kid gets it, and their face changes. That’s not a small thing.

You’re patient. You’re funny. Kids would like you. You explain things without making people feel stupid, which is rarer than it should be. You’d be good at this. Not perfect. Not immediately. But good.

I’m not saying you’re wasting your life. I’m saying you’re wasting yourself checking other people’s costings. Nine years is a long time to be bored. You don’t have to do another nine.

So: Thursday 19 November 2026, 6pm, Lewisham. Come with me. Ask your questions. Be sceptical. Bring that face you make when someone says “synergy”. If it’s rubbish, we’ll say it’s rubbish and get food after. If it’s good, you can buy me a drink and pretend you thought of it yourself.

Just don’t dismiss it from the train.

Your boy,
[Your name]

P.S. I posted it, so you have to at least read it. That’s the rule.
